I think that it will effect productions, but not in the way everyone freaks out about (killing off the incentive to create). Instead, companies will be forced to compete by retooling traditional media consumption methods as experiences instead of products:

Going to the movies won't be about seeing a movie but about hanging out with friends and getting to see a movie on equipment that is extremely cost-prohibitive to own.
Buying a game won't be about getting the game, but getting stable, easy access to the game, future updates, and social features.*
Buying physical books will be about getting the actual physical object in your hand instead a file for your tablet.
Music will be about providing something that a digital file can't. This is why vinyl has bounced back in recent years.

As long as companies adapt, they'll do fine. If they don't they'll die just like the horse-drawn carriage makers did when the car came along.

In 1916, when Minnesota Republican Harold Knutson ran for Congress the first time, he had little money, was facing a candidate who had a lot of it, and decided at the outset that he would have to do something different (and inexpensive) if he was to have a chance at winning. His solution was to take his automobile along on campaign tours and fix it so he could unobtrusively throw the carburetor or something else out of kilter, whenever he needed to. Approaching a prospective voter, he would have his machine wheeze to a halt and appeal to the voter for help. The voter would fix it, without much trouble, since nothing was seriously wrong, and then Knutson would congratulate him warmly on his knowledge of mechanics, mention casually that he was running for Congress, and then pass on to the next voter. His tactics worked. When the votes were counted on election day, his opponent, who made the rounds in a high-powered car that gave no trouble, went down to defeat.

Source:

Boller, Paul F. "On the Campaign Trail." Congressional Anecdotes. New York: Oxford UP, 1991. 122. Print.
